text:
We are a new group formed to support our Chairman, Mark Ashton, and our Prime Minister-in-waiting Nigel Farage (and Reform UK). Despite the screaming from the far-left members of groups such as Blue Action, TWTD, and this Ipswich “Collective,” the move has proven to be overwhelmingly popular with regular Town fans like us, ordinary working-class people fed up with the political establishment and desperately wanting a change of Government. 

We commend Mark Ashton's initiative to meet our future Prime Minister and lobby him in the best interests of our great club (and national game). He shouldn’t have had to apologise for doing the right thing, and the national and international media condemnation painting Farage as a racist and far right is yet more proof of how low the political establishment will sink to try and discredit our Prime Minister and Reform UK.
We are aware that the members of the far left are planning a protest to disrupt the game on Monday, arranged in part over at TWTD, and we’ll be making an announcement on this in due course.

messages.text:
My wife and I used to measure the speed of a pub in DPH drinks per hour. In my early thirties our local was 2 DPH, which is a fast pub, but as we moved out eight years later it had become a 1.5 DPH (your pint takes 45 mins to drink). The metric started to unravel when we realised that fun atmospheric pubs, problematic flat roof pubs and boring non descript pubs all had a high DPH for different reasons, but we still enjoy pre judging then measuring the DPH of a pub.

Since we’ve had kids most pubs now have a 0 DPH.

text_entities.text:
My wife and I used to measure the speed of a pub in DPH drinks per hour. In my early thirties our local was 2 DPH, which is a fast pub, but as we moved out eight years later it had become a 1.5 DPH (your pint takes 45 mins to drink). The metric started to unravel when we realised that fun atmospheric pubs, problematic flat roof pubs and boring non descript pubs all had a high DPH for different reasons, but we still enjoy pre judging then measuring the DPH of a pub.

Since we’ve had kids most pubs now have a 0 DPH.

messages.text: Was trying to workout why I feel so meh about Saturday. Think it’s cause everything about this season suggests that we’ll lose the derby, but still go up in second. It’s a season of relative consistency but just lacking moments, the real highs. Even Saturday: our first from behind win, yet there was little drama, just two quick fire first-half goals. The double over Coventry was great… but would have been all the better were we properly challenging them. The 5-0 over Sheff Utd was when they were shocking. Got turned over at Boro. First game of the season was a big occasion and we didn’t show up. Whole thing has felt like a slog. And yet… if we buck the trend and win in style on Saturday it’ll be all the sweeter. I still just don’t quite have the faith in this group, sadly.

messages.text:
Asked about the scheduling. In the past seasons have been extended to fit in games. Is there a case for that in the modern day.. 
KM I think that would be difficult for the integrity of the competition. For example if we both needed a point us and Southampton could just pass the ball around for 90 mins. 
He thinks there is something that could be done to help Championship teams who go deep in FA CUp and are still going for promotion like Southampton and Coventry last time round.

messages.text:
Very few players will play all the minutes in the coming games. will need to utilize the strength of the group. 
Jaden had some niggles in the last bit of his return from injury. Got a kick v Millwall which caused him issues. 
He is working hard and is close to being back to where he wants to be. 

Asked about Jens. He is working hard, been a difficult spell for him. Not quite hit the heights he would have hoped to. 
Lots of reasons for that. His professionalism is really good and fully engaged. 
Championship is such a tough league to play in. Jens is one who has probably found that out. 
We have massive belief in him. Capable of playing for big clubs and in Europe and he will have that chance next season when I fuck him off..

messages.text: I don’t mind this hot take. Leif has the same problem that Trent AA has, in that they started playing football about 20 years after 442 fell out of fashion. He’d be an excellent left midfielder in a 442, able to whip in crosses from the left or a killer through ball, you’re not expected to finish much, and while there’s a need to put your foot in and win the ball back as a midfielder you’ve got a left back behind you better suited to defending.

messages.text: Obv Kieran won’t play Leif on the wing. In the promotion seasons KMK adapted by - according to the heat maps - telling Leif to GTF away from the defence and join the three attacking midfielders as a line of four behind the forward. When Leif bombed on the right back shuffled over and Morsy and Mass stayed put, giving a screen of two in front of a back three. I’m surprised we weren’t countered more on the wings, it lacks width. Going forwards we have a left winger who cuts in, Jaden/JC, giving Leif the space to overlap. Not sure what’s happened with the early season experiment to have Leif cut inside.

messages.text:
KM’s comments on Kipre after Norwich (H)… Be amazed if he doesn’t start today.

"A brilliant performance. Long before the goal, when there was tension in the game on both teams, I thought he looked the most composed player on the pitch.
"It was everything we were hoping for, to be honest, because he has got that calm, laidback demeanour and in big games sometimes that can be really useful.
"Gave a real composure to the team, dealt with the threat really, really well, was calm on the ball and even better he stepped up and smashed a goal in.”

messages.text:
There was a lot of head shaking and tutting when Fabrizio Romano took the Saudi money and started tweeting how great Saudi is as a place to visit and do business. That led to a few articles analysing him and his methods and journalists denouncing him as no longer one of their own.

His business model being to accept money and send tweets/mentions on behalf of players agitating for a move, clubs wanting it look like they’re a buying club to their fans, and selling clubs wanting to drum up interest and create an auction.

…Is Alan Nixon still a journalist or is he now an EFL Romano?

If the latter, I guess there’s a difference between reading the headline and understanding why he’s written that headline. There’s probably something to learn from both but it might not be the same thing.

Are we in for Ruthsworth, are Brighton scaring other suitors to act now or is Ruthsworth’s agent linking him to the calibre of club he’d like to eventually move to?

We’ve gone from being the most average Championship of Championship clubs - 14 seasons in a row - to the pity of the Many Pauls era, to the adulation of double promotion. Now we’re favourites with evil parachute payments our rich American private equity owners are being mentioned more and expectations are raised and harder to meet. “You’ve spent how much? This all predates Farage but the last couple of weeks has probably cemented our image as whatever the opposite of a cuddly family club is.

There's two positions where most weeks there's a bit of debate about who should play which are becoming pretty clear for me for the run in.

 Kipré has been really good for most of the season but his form has fallen off a cliff the last month or so, Greaves' shirt now next to O'Shea.

And Dan Neil just hasn't been what we are after at all, lacks physicality, doesn't offer enough for the ball, and loses possession so often. Taylor far from perfect in that role but offers much more of what we need in there I think, especially whilst Matusiwa isn't 100%.

messages.text:
Happened to my local team in Spain last year and it was an absolute disaster. 

They were in a strong position to win the playoffs and in decent form, then the president made a batshit decision to get rid of the very well liked coach 2 games before the end of the season. I didn’t renew my season ticket as a result for the first time in 10 years.

Nastic went on to lose the playoff final after the new coach wanted to stamp his authority on the team and changed the tactics. He was then sacked a few months into this season and the club’s now had 3 permanent managers this season alone. And there’s a chance of going down too.

The grass most certainly isn’t always greener!

messages.text:
To be fair I don’t think many clubs recruited that well last summer in comparison. Especially those that went down. The market is so inflated right now.

I just hope we don’t go the same route again in the summer ,and spend the vast majority of our transfer fund on the UK market like we did last time we got promoted.  Signing the likes of Matusiwa is proof we can find some bargains abroad. 

Walle-Egeli hasn’t done anywhere near as well as hoped but he’s still very young and has a high ceiling. There are many examples of young players that have been signed for big money that take time to fully develop and don’t make an immediate impact. Hopefully after a full and, fingers crossed, injury free pre season he’ll start to put in improved performances.

messages.text: No need to apologise for an opinion. I’ve long stopped expecting to hear anything “real” from a press interview. If you look at us this season we’ve slowly clawed our way into second. We’ve not dominated a top two position and had Boro not totally capitulated we’d be in the playoff mix. I do think given how long KMck has been at Ipswich that we have underperformed. We’ve a large squad and yet a number of players aren’t getting minutes and a couple are noticeably going backwards. Watched a number of officials etc. going to EFL awards this evening. No Town player nominated nor the manager speaks volumes yet confuses for a team that sits second.

messages.text: I think it has been mad and chaotic in a way that I've not seen from an Ipswich side before. We have the ability to completely implode in games and see them go away from us really quickly. That's different to having a poor game, or missing a lot of players to injury or simply a piece of bad luck going against us. The team reacts badly to any sort of adversity and a game that was previously in control spirals fast out of control.

messages.text:
Also another issue is the systems of play aren't so evident. KM developed trademark moves and plays that we would pull off regularly in games to varying effect. Then we would suddenly develop another move that we added to the armoury. Example- Burns/Donacien overlaps, LD high line and crossing, Burns pull back to penalty spot for no. 10, Morsy dropped shoulder and then surge into space, Burgess long ball from back to Hirst to run through. All sorts of variety.
There is not one "go to" move that this team have developed, apart from Philogene stepping inside and shooting (which is all about the individual).

messages.text:
We’re blowing hot and cold at the moment, I don’t know which version is going to turn up for each game (or each half!).

Also the nagging feeling that we’re being propped up by some good luck - the ball crossing the line against Brum, Nunez deserving six yellows, two marginal penalty calls going for us. Perhaps we’re paying ourselves back for early season bad luck(??), just don’t want to rely on luck!

The big positive is, apart from the Soton game, we’ve got through the toughest part of our run in with our noses still in front.

When Albion’s ground lay beneath blue skies,
And Suffolk hearts beat hard though far from home,
They met the hour with fire within their eyes
As one they stood, unyielding, forged in stone.

Cometh the hour, the faithful voices cry,
Cometh the man, yet none shall stand alone,
Cometh the team, and fate itself draws nigh,
One step from glory, victory to be won.

messages.text:
So here we go, the game everyone is building up as a cup final (externally)!

If someone would have said after I watched Boro dismount Birmingham & QPR on sky a couple of months ago we would be going into last week of the season knowing a win guarantees us promotion we would have all taken it.

Yes, let’s get the job done tonight! BUT, if we lose it in whilst throwing caution to the wind then so be it. Worse case scenario we wake up tomorrow morning knowing we have to beat QPR at home Saturday.

One last snippet (😂), this will never be as well celebrated as two years ago. But let’s not take it for granted. As a 35 year old fan, I’ve only seen 3 promotions, Wembley (barely remember) and the two back to back. I will be celebrating this one just as much. Never get tired of celebrating success!

COYB

messages.text:
Think context is everything here though. Because we were playing the form team, probably the outstanding team, in the division, on their own ground, with them also having to win.
And it was only in the last 20 mins or so when it really opened up. All the stats, particularly first half, demonstrate it was a close game with limited chances for much of it.
I do agree we had a rocky period after we scored but, unlike what has characterised us in certain away games, we steadied again, especially after they had equalised.
I think KM got it right, that the team showed all of the qualities that have developed and he probably can't say "that weren't there on other occasions".

messages.text: This is Southampton 2nd goal. They do this so well. Was trying to see where the press breaks. People will ask why matusiwa is so high but he has to get attached to the deep lying CM to stop them playing out. Jens is pressing the centre half & Neil is basically having to play as 2nd left back covering the other midfielder. so they have emptied the centre of the pitch.  Notice how Manning rotates inside and that is what does us. We end up with Mcateer & furlong trying to press Azaz who slips it between them. I think ideally we want furlong to press him and have Kasey stay inside to stop the ball to Manning. Once they break that we are screwed as there is a massive hole they created. Have to say from there Manning does amazingly well to pick the pass and the boy finishes it nicely.. Hard to moan to much its the risk you take when trying to win the ball high..

2. Ipswich 82
——————
3. Millwall 81
4. Boro 80
5. Saints 78
6. Wrexham 71
——————
7. Hull 71

Early goal at Portman Road… to QPR. They’ve been fired up by the talk of them rolling over, and punish a tired-looking Ipswich with a fast start, Harvey Vale getting the goal. Ipswich are 1-0 down after 5 minutes but they remain 2nd – at least until Middlesbrough take the lead at Wrexham when Morgan Whittaker fires a shot through Danny Ward. It remains 0-0 in Millwall v Oxford and Preston v Southampton.

2. Boro 82
——————
3. Ipswich 81
4. Millwall 81
5. Saints 78
6. Hull 71
——————
7. Wrexham 70

Wrexham immediately peg Boro back, with Josh Windass the scorer. Then suddenly Millwall lead Oxford through an unfortunate Hidde ter Averst own goal, and for a short but precious period, Millwall are going up…

2. Millwall 83
——————
3. Ipswich 81
4. Boro 80
5. Saints 78
6. Wrexham 71
——————
7. Hull 71

But, as half-time approaches in their injury-affected game and when everyone else is in the dressing room, Ipswich equalise through a powerful Leif Davis daisy cutter. And then, unbelievably, just as Ipswich’s rivals prepare to kick off the second half – the stoppage has been deemed too long for everybody to have to wait – a deflected effort from range loops over a QPR defender and drops under the bar. After 45 minutes, Ipswich were 1-0 down. At half-time, it’s 2-1 to Ipswich.

2. Ipswich 84
——————
3. Millwall 83
4. Boro 80
5. Saints 78
6. Wrexham 71
——————
7. Hull 71

The second half peters out after that. Ipswich score a third, and a fourth. Millwall get a second against Oxford which doesn’t change anything. Boro, sapped of belief by scorelines elsewhere, labour in attack while nonetheless keeping out a Wrexham side who don’t lack motivation but do lack energy. But just as it looks like nothing is going to change after half-time, Hull score late on, Wrexham drop out of the play-offs and a quickfire brace for Finn Azaz means Southampton have beaten Preston and leapfrogged Boro on goal difference.

But just as it looks like nothing is going to change after half-time, Hull score late on, Wrexham drop out of the play-offs and a quickfire brace for Finn Azaz means Southampton have beaten Preston and leapfrogged Boro on goal difference.
FINAL STANDINGS

messages.text: I’ve got a nice story about Big Game Burns. My dad used to live in a village in South Wales, and Wes’ grandad used to drink in the local pub there. Most people around there are rugby fans, so he enjoyed talking to people about football. Burns was at Fleetwood at the time. Unfortunately, he passed away before Burns signed for us, but I wonder if he ever knew he’d go on to achieve everything he has in his career so far. I really hope it isn’t his last game for us today! 💙

Truly proud of this wonderful club and fanbase and how far we’ve come in such a short space of time!

We started the season looking to have a 10 who was a second striker and had the options of Szmodics and Akpom for that role; we ended it with the minutes shared between Nunez and Mehmeti so absolutely a stylistic mistake at the start that was corrected.

He was relegated to small cameos, but is a big, strong, physical boy with a good touch and gets around the pitch - but don't think can judge him too much of his spell here by the end of the season.

Issue we have is it will be a 3 year deal on decent money, but the logic of the signing and how it was structured made sense at the time.

Ultimately, will be a low risk move even on good wages for someone to pick up next season and if they can unlock his goals then it will more than pay for itself so someone will do so

messages.text:
* [2:10 can you stay in the PL?] we're looking at what brentford, brighton and sunderland have done. we need a different approach around player recruitment this year. investors have said they'll back us to the hilt.
* simon jordan says something egotistical whilst looking like a scarecrow on the run from interpol in the south of spain
* [4:15 what are the lessons to learn from last time in the PL?] last time commercial revenues and wider infrastructure wasn't up to scratch after 20 years out of the PL. now everything is better; performance, medical, data. new training facilities. our backroom staff are great, the availability of our players end of season was excellent. but ultimately we need good recruitment. (translation: we bought shit players last time and we'll try not to do that again.)
* [5:31 will kieran stay?] errrr.... waffle... he's good... nothing of substance. we are well set to take this club forwards. 😬
* [6:20 will you start the season with kieran mckenna?] "in my mind, yes." 😬😬 kieran and i have started to make plans, work on pre-season, we're tired after last season. kieran is great.
* simon jordan says nothing of note in a vaguely threatening manner.
* [8:40 are you going to spend £140m again?] we also sold £80m-£90m when we were relegated, so we trade a lot. we're fishing in a small pond. we've built a brand new recruitment dept. we don't recruit just based off data.
* [9:30 did you support the expansion of the Ch play offs?] yes we voted for it, it was mostly unanimous.

I remember him as a battering ram, give him the ball and he charges as far as he can before he’s brought to the ground, like a rugby player driving forwards. It creates space behind him but I hear you, I doubt KMK started our PL season with ‘absolute chaos’ as one of his intended patterns of play.

text.text: Revealed: Full details of ‘Southampton’s spying mission’ to Middlesbrough

text: Middlesbrough believe they were the victims of a highly professional surveillance operation after catching a man filming a training session before their play-off semi-final against Southampton.

can reveal the full details of the alleged attempt to steal training-ground secrets ahead of Saturday’s crucial match.

The “spy” had professional surveillance equipment, complete with a microphone to record voices and technology to livestream the footage back to someone watching remotely.

A brief physical confrontation ensued when a member of Middlesbrough’s media team challenged the man, who refused to identify himself and then ran off.

The man ran into the clubhouse next to the training ground and changed into new clothes from a hidden holdall.

Middlesbrough have since been told by whistleblowers that this is not the first time a member of Southampton’s analyst team has been sent to record opposition training sessions this season.

CCTV footage has been studied by the club and the alleged perpetrator has been identified. He is said to be an analyst on Southampton’s website and has worked for the club for more than a year, having held similar positions at Premier League clubs.

Middlesbrough have informed the

that they view this as a clear and obvious case of cheating and are seeking the harshest possible punishment. A wide range of action is possible when dealing with cases such as these, including points deductions, fines and potential expulsion from the play-offs.

The Middlesbrough hierarchy are furious after a member of their own media team allegedly spotted the man filming the session, masked by some bushes, on the adjacent golf course attached to Rockcliffe Hotel.

It is claimed the man filming the session had professional filming equipment, complete with a microphone powerful enough to pick up the voice of manager Kim Hellberg and his coaching staff as they issued training instructions.
have been contacted for comment regarding these new accusations but did not respond.

text.text: Boro believe opponents know their starting XI

text:
Given the importance of Saturday’s game and the financial rewards on offer if either club win promotion to the Premier League, Middlesbrough have stressed the seriousness of the situation and the level of potential harm done.

Thursday’s training is the last detailed session before the game and they believe the man was sent to gain the most damaging information which would have included team selection, shape, tactical instructions as well as set-piece routines.

With that in mind, the club feel they are already at a big disadvantage heading into the two-legged tie and they believe their opponents are already aware of their starting XI for the first leg. If they change it, they would not be picking the manager’s first-choice side.

Middlesbrough are awaiting an update from the EFL before deciding their next move but

understands nothing is off the table.

The EFL released a statement on Thursday night saying it had “written to Southampton FC requesting their observations following a complaint from Middlesbrough FC relating to alleged unauthorised filming”.

The statement continued: “The alleged incident is said to have taken place on Middlesbrough’s private property by an individual identified to be associated with Southampton.

“The League is treating this matter as potential misconduct under EFL Regulations and will be making no further comment at this time.”

The deadline for those observations to be returned to the EFL was set at 1pm on Friday but Southampton are accused of missing it.

Middlesbrough suspect their Championship rivals are playing for time and hope to avoid admitting any wrongdoing until after the game on Saturday.

The EFL has the scope to hand out severe punishments for clubs found guilty of spying on opposition teams after changing the rules in the wake of spying scandal at Leeds United in 2019.

text: Leeds were fined after then manager Marcelo Bielsa

text.text: admitted that he had sent spies to watch a Derby County training session

text:
before a match between the two sides. At the time, no such rule prevented it, but Leeds were fined £200,000 over breaches of good faith.

The EFL subsequently created a new rule that prohibits any team viewing their opposition’s training sessions up to 72 hours before a game.

Shaun Harvey, then EFL chief executive, said at the time: “The sanctions imposed highlight how actions such as this cannot be condoned and act as a clear deterrent should any club seek to undertake poor conduct in the future.”

Middlesbrough privately believe a fine would not be much of a deterrent in this case given the benefits of gaining an unfair advantage ahead of a game of this magnitude.

They will push for the harshest possible sanction with owner Steve Gibson probably set to raise the matter directly with his Southampton counterparts in the Riverside boardroom on Saturday.

The EFL has been contacted for comment in relation to the fresh allegations made against Southampton.

messages.text:
The inside story of ‘Spygate’ — featuring a pine tree, disguises, damning WhatsApps and a sport in shock
By Tom Burrows, Dan Sheldon, Matt Slater, Philip Buckingham and Jordan Campbell
May 20, 2026 9:00 am GMT+1

It all started behind a pine tree.

The setting was Middlesbrough’s Rockliffe Park training ground, two days before the club were due to meet Southampton in the Championship play-off semi-finals.

Will Salt, a first team performance analyst intern working for Southampton, had travelled north to gather intelligence on the club’s opponents as they trained a few metres away beyond a metal fence. He stationed himself behind the tree and got out his mobile phone to record Middlesbrough’s players, hoping he would go unnoticed.

Advertisement


It didn’t work. Salt was spotted and, while he quickly made his escape, he had sparked into motion a story which must now rank as one of the most extraordinary in the history of the English Football League.


The view Will Salt had from behind the pine tree outside Middlesbrough’s training groundPhil Buckingham/The Athletic
It culminated on Tuesday with Southampton being expelled from the Championship play-off final. Middlesbrough, who they defeated in the semi-final, will now play Hull City on Saturday in a match worth around £200million, the rough value of a place in the Premier League.

After they admitted to spying on Middlesbrough, as well as Oxford United and Ipswich Town earlier in the season, Southampton were also given a four-point deduction that applies to next season in the Championship. The club has lodged an appeal, which will be heard by one senior judge today. The panel’s decision could yet be reversed.

It has also emerged that:

Incriminating WhatsApp messages to Southampton’s analysts from head coach Tonda Eckert were revealed in the hearing, with the German now potentially facing his own serious Football Association charges
Southampton had initially planned for Salt to go back and spy on Middlesbrough for a second day
When Southampton spied on Ipswich, the operation involved dressing in Eastleigh kit as a disguise
Southampton’s players have been left furious and are exploring legal options, including possible class action, if the verdict is upheld
Hull City are also deeply unhappy, as their preparations have been thrown into disarray, having spent four training sessions focusing on playing Southampton.
Sources at Southampton said the club were blindsided by last night’s decision, which they consider disproportionate and unprecedented. They are continuing to prepare for Saturday’s final as planned and are confident of overturning the decision. Middlesbrough, meanwhile, welcomed what they called “a clear message for the future of our game regarding sporting integrity and conduct” in a statement on their website.

The Athletic has spoken to multiple sources with knowledge of the situation, all of whom asked to remain anonymous to protect their positions, to piece together the inside story of ‘Spygate’, one of football’s most incendiary stories — and one which is not over yet.

Tuesday’s hearing was conducted remotely but featured all the drama of a classic courtroom thriller.

Southampton were represented by Kate Gallafent KC, an experienced lawyer who has worked with the FA on multiple occasions; the EFL was represented by Brendan Kelly KC, a criminal barrister with a formidable reputation in cross-examination.

Advertisement


One of the key revelations at Tuesday’s hearing were the WhatsApp messages sent by Eckert to his analysts that people with knowledge of proceedings said were particularly damaging to Southampton’s case.

Two of the club’s analysts gave evidence at the hearing in which they expressed remorse for their actions but said they were pushed into the spying trips. In his evidence, Eckert — who has spent most of his coaching career in Germany — claimed he was not aware that such behaviour was against the rules in England as it was widespread in European football.

messages.text:
The hearing was told that Eckert had sent people to spy on fellow Championship sides Oxford and Ipswich but had been displeased with the quality of their findings. In the case of Ipswich, the subterfuge extended to using kit worn by Eastleigh, whose Hampshire training ground was hosting Southampton’s opponents.

Southampton lost 2-1 away at Oxford and drew 2-2 at home to Ipswich.


Will Salt is captured recording Middlesbrough’s sessionThe Athletic
After qualifying for the play-offs, Southampton booked Salt to stay for two nights in Middlesbrough and the plan was for him to go back to the training ground for a second day until he was spotted, confronted and ran from the premises.

Eckert could now face charges, too. The FA was not commenting on possible action last night but there is precedent in football. At the 2024 Olympic Games, Canada used a drone to spy on New Zealand, their upcoming opponents in the women’s football. In that case, Canada lost six points, while their coach, Bev Priestman, along with analyst Joseph Lombardi and assistant coach Jasmine Mander, were handed a one-year ban from football by FIFA.

The Athletic has been told that a key point in the EFL’s argument was for the play-offs to be regarded as a separate knockout competition, distinct from the league season. That helps explain the two separate punishments: expulsion from the play-offs and a points deduction for next season’s league campaign.

Advertisement


Southampton’s squad, who had been given a few days off after their second-leg win, had largely been kept away from the affair, with only the basic details communicated to them by the club.

Following Tuesday night’s news, players were understandably angry — only finding out via a text message sent by the club at the same time as the news broke more widely.

There was an added factor, as players who had taken 40 per cent pay cuts after suffering relegation from the top flight year were due to have that reinstated in the event of promotion. They will train on Wednesday as planned but multiple players are understood to be exploring their legal options, including possible class action, if the verdict is upheld.

The Athletic has contacted Southampton for comment.

It may have ended in a virtual hearing, but ‘Spygate’ began at Rockcliffe Park, an unlikely backdrop for industrial espionage.

Set in the County Durham countryside, Middlesbrough’s training ground nestles between a golf course and hotel on one side and a cricket club on another, all contained in a gentle horseshoe bend of the River Tees.

Salt’s chosen vantage point, with a clear view of the two first-team pitches 100 or so yards away, was next to a road that snakes down from the five-star Rockcliffe Hall hotel to the golf course’s clubhouse. A metal farm gate next to the tree Salt hid behind carries the sign “Private property, authorised personnel only” but there is little privacy. No high fences or hedges. A clear, unbroken view.

All of the land — training ground, hotel and golf course — belongs to Middlesbrough owner Steve Gibson and his Bulkhaul business partner Mike O’Neill but its public nature, welcoming hundreds of guests each day, allowed Salt access to the area where he was photographed.


The golf course where Salt fled after being caught spyingPhil Buckingham/The Athletic
The image of Salt, obtained by The Athletic and other media outlets, showed him half-hidden by the tree, holding up his mobile phone while wearing wireless headphones. Middlesbrough staff are known to have approached Salt as he filmed but he soon left the scene, heading to the golf course clubhouse a short distance away.

messages.text:
It is alleged he changed his clothes in the wood-panelled locker room in the clubhouse before leaving the scene on foot.

Middlesbrough quickly lodged a complaint with the EFL and Southampton were duly charged the following day with two breaches of their regulations, with the case being referred to an Independent Disciplinary Commission.

The play-off semi-final first leg ended goalless. Some fans made light of the affair by dressing in camouflage and holding up binoculars and one source told The Athletic that Phil Parsons, Southampton’s CEO, had a conciliatory conversation with Gibson at the Riverside stadium.


A Middlesbrough fan makes his point to Southampton before the play-off semi-final first legEd Sykes/Getty Images
Even so, tensions behind the scenes were beginning to bubble up. In the post-match press conference, Eckert and the club’s head of communications, Jordan Sibley, walked out after refusing to answer any further questions relating to spying.

Meanwhile, Middlesbrough head coach Kim Hellberg didn’t hold back in his post-match press conference, accusing Southampton of cheating. “Every team in the Championship should be angry. It is wrong, it is wrong,” he told reporters.

Middlesbrough, meanwhile, had started to compile a dossier of evidence and hired high-profile sports lawyer Nick De Marco KC to build their case.

The club trawled their records to find details of a credit card used by Salt at the golf club. They also said they had a written statement from a former Southampton employee which alleged the Middlesbrough spying incident was far from a one-off.

The Athletic had been told by multiple sources that Southampton had attempted to spy on Oxford at their training centre on Christmas Eve, before the clubs’ meeting at the Kassam Stadium on Boxing Day. Oxford had sacked Gary Rowett, their head coach, on December 23, which meant Craig Short led the side on an interim basis for that Southampton game — potentially prompting a change of tactics.

Advertisement


In the EFL statement last night, it was confirmed that Southampton had admitted to the hearing that they had spied on Oxford, as well as on Ipswich in April 2026.

Barring a short statement acknowledging their charge, Southampton kept their counsel, only going public on May 12, the day of the semi-final second leg at St Mary’s, when Parsons issued a statement, saying the club was “fully cooperating with the EFL and the Disciplinary Commission, whilst also undertaking an internal review to ensure that all facts and context are properly understood”.


Southampton admitted to spying on Oxford before this game on Boxing DayBradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
The second leg was even more bad-tempered than the first. Southampton fans threw missiles at Middlesbrough’s team coach as it arrived at the stadium and the game itself was marred by a confrontation between the visitors’ Luke Ayling and Southampton’s Taylor Harwood-Bellis, with the latter allegedly making reference to the Middlesbrough defender’s speech impediment.

When Southampton scored their late winner from Shea Charles, Harwood-Bellis celebrated with a binoculars gesture in front of Middlesbrough’s Aidan Morris.

In the press conferences that followed, Eckert again walked out early with their head of communications when a reporter asked, “Are you a cheat?” In response, the head of communications told the reporter: “Let’s show some respect.”

Hellberg was visibly emotional after the defeat, describing the situation as “disgraceful” adding that it “breaks my heart.”

The row even went political when Andy McDonald, the Member of Parliament for Middlesbrough and Thornaby East, called for Southampton to lose their spot in the play-off final.

The most dramatic twist yet, however, came the next day, Wednesday, May 13, when the photograph of Salt emerged, initially via the Daily Mail.

Southampton fans threw missiles at Middlesbrough’s team coach as it arrived at the stadium and the game itself was marred by a confrontation between the visitors’ Luke Ayling and Southampton’s Taylor Harwood-Bellis, with the latter allegedly making reference to the Middlesbrough defender’s speech impediment.

When Southampton scored their late winner from Shea Charles, Harwood-Bellis celebrated with a binoculars gesture in front of Middlesbrough’s Aidan Morris.

In the press conferences that followed, Eckert again walked out early with their head of communications when a reporter asked, “Are you a cheat?” In response, the head of communications told the reporter: “Let’s show some respect.”

Hellberg was visibly emotional after the defeat, describing the situation as “disgraceful” adding that it “breaks my heart.”

The row even went political when Andy McDonald, the Member of Parliament for Middlesbrough and Thornaby East, called for Southampton to lose their spot in the play-off final.

The most dramatic twist yet, however, came the next day, Wednesday, May 13, when the photograph of Salt emerged, initially via the Daily Mail.

messages.text:
It underlined that far from being an act of sophisticated subterfuge, it was the most basic of operations, leading many to wonder just how much value his intelligence could have added to Southampton’s preparations.

Advertisement


Until then, Salt had only once been pictured on Southampton’s website, as part of an image of Eckert and his staff celebrating a manager of the month award, but now he found himself at the centre of a storm.

He had returned to work at Southampton’s Staplewood training ground that same day after being given a few days off, with sources describing him as being quiet and keeping his head down. His phone had been examined by Southampton’s lawyers as they sifted through evidence.

The EFL confirmed that the independent hearing would be heard by Tuesday (May 19), but behind the scenes there were convoluted negotiations taking place around who could contribute to it and how.

While the case itself was between Southampton and the EFL, Middlesbrough were adamant they wanted to be in the room to make their case through De Marco. From the start, Boro wanted to pursue a sporting sanction against Southampton — namely, ejection from the play-offs, a point they made in a public statement on the Friday night.

The EFL, meanwhile, was resistant to any notion that the play-off final could be delayed. It was wary of being seen to ‘pre-judge’ the outcome of the case if it pushed back the game, while postponing would also present a raft of broadcasting, commercial and logistical problems.


Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert may face his own disciplinary actionJasper Wax/Getty Images
Boro were ultimately denied the right to attend the hearing but were permitted to make a written submission as an interested party. While they did not have the right to appeal the decision, they would have been able to pursue compensation from Southampton. In the meantime, the club went about business as usual, with players reporting back for training on May 18 to prepare for a possible play-off final.

Southampton, for their part, were not denying that spying had taken place but were growing increasingly concerned about what they perceived as due process not being followed. The club felt that such cases would routinely see clubs offered 14 days to answer a charge.

Advertisement


Club sources told The Athletic that they felt the hearing should have taken place after the final, rather than being expedited by the EFL. They thought there were too many rules that had no defined sanctions, which left too much open to interpretation, and if the rules had been clearer, the incident would have been resolved more speedily.

They pointed out that Southampton put in one of their worst performances in recent months against Middlesbrough in the first leg — especially in the first half — which suggested that no sporting advantage had been gained.

They also made the point that the most obvious precedent, when Leeds United were caught spying on Derby County in 2019, had resulted in the Yorkshire club being fined £200,000.

There was, of course, another team caught in the middle of the spat: Hull City.

After defeating Millwall 2-0 at The Den on May 11 to book their place at Wembley, the East Yorkshire club found themselves not knowing for sure which team they should be preparing to face at Wembley.

In an interview with The Athletic, Hull head coach Sergej Jakirovic warned against his side becoming “collateral damage”, but acknowledged that he had been preparing to meet Southampton.

They have now completed four training sessions, preparing for Southampton, only to find themselves having to switch opponents less than four days before the final. Hull’s players and backroom staff are due to travel south to London tomorrow. Defeat at Wembley could provoke more recriminations.


Hull have been expecting to play SouthamptonTony King/Getty Images
Away from the football, Hull have been left unhappy at the handling of the situation.

messages.text:
Although sympathetic to the EFL’s position initially, the continued uncertainty over the date of the game has made planning difficult for the club’s supporters, who are yet to sell their full allocation. Southampton had already sold out their 37,000 share which will now need to be refunded, presenting another logistical headache.

Advertisement


In a statement on Friday, the Hull City official supporters’ club said the EFL “could and should have had a more robust system in place to deal with this eventuality, one that does not punish innocent fans who should be enjoying contemplating seeing their club play at the national stadium”.

The judgment, when it was announced at 6:45pm on Tuesday, sent shockwaves through the sport — probably best summarised by Steve Parish, the Crystal Palace chairman, who posted an exploding head emoji on X.

Others revelled in Southampton’s misery, with local rivals Portsmouth posting a message saying the south coast derby was ‘coming soon’. Meanwhile, on Google Maps, an aerial image of Middlesbrough’s training ground now comes with an added feature: Tonda Eckert Bush.

Yet there could still be a sting in the tail, in the shape of Southampton’s appeal. That will be heard on Wednesday afternoon, with the verdict expected to be delivered in the evening.

Both sides are confident that their argument will prevail, yet the truth is this is unprecedented territory. What happens next could shape not just the make-up of next season’s Premier League, but football’s legal foundations.

text:
This is the EFL Independent Disciplinary Commission’s written decision on Southampton FC’s admitted breaches for observing opposition training sessions.

The case centred on three incidents:

Southampton-associated personnel were observed near Middlesbrough’s training ground before the play-off semi-final. Middlesbrough complained to the EFL with photographic evidence. Southampton later progressed past Middlesbrough 2-1 on aggregate, with the second leg decided in extra time.
The same individual observed Oxford training before Southampton played them on Boxing Day. Information and footage were shared with Southampton. Southampton lost that fixture 2-1.

On the day Southampton played Ipswich, a Southampton-associated individual attended Eastleigh FC, where Ipswich were training. The Commission says this was done on instructions from Southampton coaching and analytical staff, and the footage/information was shared internally. The match ended 2-2.  

Southampton admitted all six charges: three breaches of
, requiring clubs to act with “utmost good faith”, and three breaches of

, which prohibits clubs from directly or indirectly observing another club’s training session within 72 hours of a match between the clubs.  

Southampton’s defence was effectively: yes, we breached the rules, but we gained no material sporting advantage, so a fine or reduced points penalty would be enough. They also relied on mitigation: cooperation with the EFL, admissions, remorse, and the precedent of Leeds United’s 2019 “spygate” case, which resulted in a £200,000 fine and reprimand.  

The Commission rejected that. It found this was not innocent or low-level behaviour, but a

text.text: “contrived and determined plan from the top down”

text:
to gain a competitive advantage by collecting tactical and selection information. It was particularly critical of Southampton using junior staff or interns to carry out the observations under pressure.  

The key legal/sporting point is this: the Commission said

text.text: sporting advantage does not need to equal sporting success

text:
. In other words, Southampton did not need to win the match, change their tactics, or demonstrably benefit on the pitch for the breach to matter. The Commission’s position was that obtaining private information about team selection, injuries, formation or preparation is itself a sporting advantage.  

The play-off element made the sanction much harsher. The Commission said a points deduction or fine might work in a regular-season case, but in the play-offs the financial reward of Premier League promotion is so large that a fine could become meaningless. It said allowing a fine-only sanction could effectively incentivise clubs to cheat if promotion was at stake.  

The final sanctions were:

text.text: Southampton expelled from the 2025/26 Championship Play-Offs. Middlesbrough to play Hull City in the final.
Four-point deduction for Southampton at the start of 2026/27

text: , covering the Oxford and Ipswich incidents.
, especially because junior staff were put under pressure to do something they considered morally wrong.

The case centred on three incidents:
Middlesbrough incident — 7 May 2026

Oxford United incident — 23/24 December 2025
The same individual observed Oxford training before Southampton played them on Boxing Day. Information and footage were shared with Southampton. Southampton lost that fixture 2-1.
Ipswich Town incident — 28 April 2026

On the day Southampton played Ipswich, a Southampton-associated individual attended Eastleigh FC, where Ipswich were training. The Commission says this was done on instructions from Southampton coaching and analytical staff, and the footage/information was shared internally. The match ended 2-2.  

Southampton admitted all six charges: three breaches of
Regulation 3.4
, requiring clubs to act with “utmost good faith”, and three breaches of
Regulation 127

, which prohibits clubs from directly or indirectly observing another club’s training session within 72 hours of a match between the clubs.  

Southampton’s defence was effectively: yes, we breached the rules, but we gained no material sporting advantage, so a fine or reduced points penalty would be enough. They also relied on mitigation: cooperation with the EFL, admissions, remorse, and the precedent of Leeds United’s 2019 “spygate” case, which resulted in a £200,000 fine and reprimand.  

The Commission rejected that. It found this was not innocent or low-level behaviour, but a
“contrived and determined plan from the top down”

to gain a competitive advantage by collecting tactical and selection information. It was particularly critical of Southampton using junior staff or interns to carry out the observations under pressure.  

The key legal/sporting point is this: the Commission said
sporting advantage does not need to equal sporting success

. In other words, Southampton did not need to win the match, change their tactics, or demonstrably benefit on the pitch for the breach to matter. The Commission’s position was that obtaining private information about team selection, injuries, formation or preparation is itself a sporting advantage.  

The play-off element made the sanction much harsher. The Commission said a points deduction or fine might work in a regular-season case, but in the play-offs the financial reward of Premier League promotion is so large that a fine could become meaningless. It said allowing a fine-only sanction could effectively incentivise clubs to cheat if promotion was at stake.  

The final sanctions were:
Southampton expelled from the 2025/26 Championship Play-Offs. Middlesbrough to play Hull City in the final.
Four-point deduction for Southampton at the start of 2026/27
, covering the Oxford and Ipswich incidents.

, especially because junior staff were put under pressure to do something they considered morally wrong.

messages.text:
I met Gazza just after he did his knee in 1991. He was doing a fishing video near Ely in Cambs where I grew up. We found out and went and waited by his hotel. I was 11 at the time.

Anyway he comes home from a days fishing to be met by 4 kids and our parents. He was delighted to see us. Told us to wait while he went and showered. He comes back out 20 mins later loaded with gifts, posters for us and stopped and hung out with us. He also played footy with us and was doing keepy puppy whilst his knee was in a brace! I was completely starstruck, and he was everything an 11 year old would want their hero to be.

's name has surfaced . It hasn't been a good season for the Colombian, who, between injuries and an adjustment period, hasn't delivered the performance expected by the coaching staff. However,

, the club is convinced that a sale would generate a profit, after numerous teams inquired about his availability.
Besides River Plate, where Chacho Coudet holds him in high regard, and various Brazilian teams - Flamengo and Vasco da Gama - the latest club to inquire about the Colombian's situation has been

, a newly promoted Premier League team that wants to make a significant investment for the upcoming season.
In the last two seasons, the English club has invested heavily in signings, even last season after their relegation to the Championship, and now they want to strengthen their midfield to try and establish themselves in the top flight. Deossa's name was highly regarded in the European market after his strong performance at the Club World Cup, although the Colombian ultimately chose Betis over other options such as West Ham, who have just been relegated.
At Betis, the player's market value is clear, even though he hasn't performed as expected for the club, and they intend to make a profit.

With this scenario in mind, Betis is waiting for the bidding war for Deossa to begin. The Premier League's financial power, should the interest from Ipswich Town or even West Ham materialize, would drive up the Colombian's price tag, but there are also indications from South America that they have the funds to enter the market. "It's the first time since I've been here that I'll be able to participate and choose players with the characteristics I think I need to play the way I want to play. There will certainly be movement; I think we'll have an active role in the market and we'll be able to put together something really nice," said Coudet, River Plate's manager, regarding his expectations for reinforcements this summer.
The expected income from Deossa, which would also free up a non-EU player spot, would be added to other deals to secure the funds needed to close out the financial year. The names of Sergi Altimira, valued at €25 million, and Pablo García are also under consideration, although the sporting director is hoping for moves involving more players from the squad.

text.text: But it’s not as simple as saying that PSG are a better side than Arsenal, or even that they are a better attacking side. They are a much fresher side. Only one of their players, Vitinha, had played more than 2000 minutes of league football this season; nine of Arsenal’s had. PSG were able to rest players for league games secure in the knowledge that their squad is by far the best in Ligue Un; their wage bill is almost double that of the side with the second-biggest, Marseille, and 10 times that of, say, Le Havre. Arsenal do not have that luxury; for them every game had the potential to be a scrap, and that is exhausting. Swap the squads round and PSG would probably still be the side playing with verve.

text: Bright Path Sports Partners is a private equity firm founded in 2022 that focuses on routing Native American and institutional capital into professional sports franchises. [

Backed by billionaire and Native American funds, Bright Path finalized a deal totaling up to $154 million (£120 million) for a 44% stake in Gamechanger 20 Ltd., the holding company that owns Ipswich Town. [

The PE firm's entry into the club coincided with a massive rise in value; Ipswich Town FC was valued at roughly £350 million—the highest valuation ever recorded for an EFL Championship side prior to their Premier League promotion. [
